modules.title: Module 1 — English Phrasal Verbs
modules.description: Phrasal verbs are an essential part of spoken and written English at all levels. Phrasal verbs are combinations of ordinary verbs, like put, take, come, and go, and words like in, out, on, and off. In other situations, the words like in, out, on, and off are called prepositions and adverbs, but in phrasal verbs we call them particles because they are not doing the job of prepositions and adverbs (but sometimes we also use prepositions with phrasal verbs). Many phrasal verbs are idiomatic. Idiomatic means that there is no way to know what the verb and particle mean together by knowing what the verb and particle mean separately.

topics.title: Daily routines, rest and leisure
topics.context:
These phrasal verbs describe sleep, free time, routines, and everyday behaviour. Each entry gives the meaning used in this topic and an example.

### Sleep and daily routine
- **wake up**: stop sleeping. *I woke up at six, but stayed in bed until seven.*
- **get up**: get out of bed or rise to your feet. *I got up as soon as the alarm rang.*
- **stay up**: remain awake instead of going to bed. *We stayed up late to watch the final.*
- **stay out**: remain away from home. *The teenagers stayed out until midnight on Saturday.*
- **doze off / nod off**: fall into a light sleep unintentionally; these are interchangeable for this meaning. *I nodded off during the film.*

### Rest and leisure
- **chill out**: relax and take it easy (informal). *We chilled out at home after work.*
- **kick back**: relax and enjoy your free time (informal). *On Sunday, I kicked back with a book.*
- **lie around**: recline and do very little. *I lay around all morning on my day off.*
- **hang out**: spend relaxed, informal time in a place or with people (informal). *They hang out at the café after class.*
- **hang around**: stay somewhere, often while waiting or passing time (informal). *We hung around outside until the doors opened.*

### Socialising and behaviour
- **drop in**: visit someone without arranging it in advance. *Feel free to drop in when you are nearby.*
- **fool around**: waste time doing silly or unimportant things. *Stop fooling around and finish your work.*
- **goof around**: play or waste time in a silly way (informal; similar to fool around). *The students were goofing around instead of studying.*
- **mess around**: waste time doing unimportant things; it can also mean handle something carelessly. *They were messing around when they should have been working.*
- **act up**: misbehave, or (of a machine/body part) cause problems. *The children acted up during the lesson.*
- **drop out**: leave a school, course, or programme before finishing it. *She dropped out of college in her second year.*
- **kick out**: force or order someone to leave a place or group. *The club kicked him out for starting a fight.*
- **hurry up**: do something or move faster. *We hurried up so we would not miss the bus.*

### Calls and practical situations
- **hang on**: wait briefly, especially on the phone; it can also mean hold tightly. *Hang on while I check the train times.*
- **hang up**: end a telephone call. *He hung up before I could say goodbye.*
- **mess up**: make a mistake, spoil a plan, or make a place untidy. *I messed up the booking and had to call the hotel.*

Watch out: **wake up** means stop sleeping, while **get up** means leave your bed or rise to your feet. **Stay up** means remain awake; **stay out** means remain away from home. **Fool around**, **goof around**, and **mess around** can all describe wasting time, but use the specific context to make the intended phrase clear.

topics.title: Food, personal care and health
topics.context:
Phrasal verbs are essential when talking about meals, clothing, personal grooming, and physical health.

### Food & Kitchen
- **heat up**: make food hotter. *I will heat up the soup in the microwave.*
- **pig out**: eat large amounts of food greedily. *We pigged out on pizza during the match.*
- **use up**: consume the entire supply of something. *Don't use up all the milk.*

### Clothing & Appearance
- **put on / take off**: dress in or remove clothing. *Put on your jacket before leaving, and take off your boots inside.*
- **try on**: test clothing for fit or style. *You should try on the shirt before buying it.*
- **dress up**: wear formal clothing or a costume. *Everyone dressed up for the gala.*
- **grow out of / grow up**: become too big for clothes, stop a habit as you mature, or develop from childhood into adulthood. *Kids grow out of sneakers fast, and many grow out of their fear of the dark.*

### Physical Well-being & Health
- **warm up**: prepare your muscles before exercise. *Always warm up before running.*
- **come down with**: start catching an illness. *I am coming down with a cold.*
- **pass out**: faint or lose consciousness; it can also mean distribute something to a group. *He passed out from the extreme heat.* *The teacher passed out the worksheets.*
- **pass away**: die (polite euphemism). *Her grandfather passed away peacefully.*
- **throw up**: vomit. *Bad seafood caused him to throw up.*

### Watch out!
- Do not confuse **pass out** (to faint) with **pass away** (to die).
- **Put on** is the opposite of **take off**, but **put on** can also mean gaining weight.

topics.title: Communication, information and understanding
topics.context:
Effective communication in English relies heavily on phrasal verbs to share information, hold conversations, exchange opinions, and solve problems.

### Conversations & Speaking
- **bring up**: raise a topic for discussion. *He brought up the budget during the meeting.*
- **blurt out**: reveal something impulsively. *She blurted out the answer before thinking.*
- **butt in**: interrupt rudely. *Don't butt in while others are speaking.*
- **talk into / talk out of**: persuade someone to do or not do something. *They talked him into joining, but talked her out of leaving.*
- **talk down to**: speak condescendingly. *Never talk down to junior colleagues.*

### Information, Investigating & Understanding
- **find out / figure out**: discover facts or solve a problem. *We found out the truth and figured out a solution.*
- **look into**: investigate an issue. *Management will look into the customer's complaint.*
- **point out**: highlight an important detail. *The auditor pointed out three major mistakes.*
- **make out**: discern with difficulty. *I could barely make out the sign in the dark.*
- **make of**: interpret or form an opinion. *What do you make of the new policy?*
- **track down**: find after a diligent search. *She tracked down the missing document.*

### Watch out!
- Do not confuse **bring up** (mention a topic or raise children) with **bring back** (return something or evoke memories).
- **Make out** refers to perception or comprehension under difficulty, whereas **figure out** involves reasoning and solving a puzzle.
### Additional high-frequency phrases
- **call back**: return a phone call. *I’ll call you back after the meeting.*
- **call for**: require something, or make it appropriate. *This urgent problem calls for a quick response.*
- **fill in**: complete a form, or give someone missing information. *Please fill in this form; I’ll fill you in on the changes later.*
- **fill up**: fill a tank/container, or eat enough to feel full. *We filled up the car and filled up on snacks.*
- **follow up (on)**: take further action or check what happened. *I’ll follow up on your request tomorrow.*
- **make for**: contribute to a result, or move towards a place. *Good teamwork makes for better results; we made for the exit.*
- **shut off**: stop a machine or cut off a supply. *Shut off the water before repairing the pipe.*
- **shut up**: stop speaking (informal, often rude). *The children finally shut up when the film began.*
- **stand for**: represent, or tolerate (usually in negative statements). *What does BBC stand for? I won’t stand for bullying.*
- **stand up**: rise to your feet; **stand someone up** means fail to meet them as planned. *We stood up when she entered, but he stood me up on Friday.*
- **tell apart**: recognize the difference between similar things. *I can’t tell the twins apart.*
- **tell on**: report someone’s wrongdoing to an authority. *The child told on his brother.*

topics.title: Relationships, progress and setbacks
topics.context:
Interpersonal relationships, professional progress, and temporary setbacks frequently feature phrasal verbs in conversational English.

### Relationships & Social Connections
- **get along with**: maintain harmonious relationships. *I get along well with my coworkers.*
- **count on**: rely on someone for dependable support. *You can always count on her.*
- **fall out with**: argue and damage a friendship. *They fell out over business decisions.*
- **get together**: meet socially to spend time together. *Let's get together for lunch soon.*
- **fall for**: become infatuated or fall in love. *He fell for her immediately.*

### Progress, Effort & Accomplishment
- **get ahead**: achieve career and personal advancement. *Dedicated study helps you get ahead.*
- **get by**: manage or survive with limited resources. *We can get by on modest savings.*
- **get around to**: finally find time for a delayed task. *I will get around to those repairs.*
- **get through**: endure an ordeal or finish a volume of work. *Faith got him through the crisis.*

### Setbacks & Difficulties
- **fall apart**: crumble physically or collapse emotionally. *The agreement fell apart.*
- **fall behind / get behind**: lag behind schedule or cohort. *Don't fall behind in coursework.*
- **fall through**: fail to happen or cancel. *Our vacation plans fell through.*
- **get down**: discourage or depress someone. *Don't let minor setbacks get you down.*
- **get over**: recover from illness or heartbreak. *She needed time to get over the loss.*

### Watch out!
- Do not confuse **fall through** (a deal that fails to happen) with **fall apart** (an existing system or object breaking into pieces).
- **Count on** means to rely upon, while **count up** means to calculate a total number.
### Additional phrases
- **fall off**: decrease in amount or level. *Sales fell off after the holidays.*
- **fall over**: lose balance and land on the ground. *He fell over on the icy path.*
- **get at**: imply or try to say something indirectly. *What are you getting at?*
- **get away (with)**: escape from a place, or avoid punishment. *The thief got away, but he won’t get away with it.*
- **get back**: return to a place; **get back at**: take revenge; **get back to**: reply later. *She got back late, then got back to me the next day; he wanted to get back at his rival.*
- **get off on**: find something especially exciting or enjoyable (informal). *He gets off on taking risks.*
- **get out of**: avoid a duty or obligation. *She tried to get out of doing the paperwork.*
- **get over**: recover from or move past something. *It took him weeks to get over the disappointment.*
- **get something over with**: finish an unpleasant experience as quickly as possible. *Let’s get the interview over with.*

topics.title: Social interaction, attitudes and choices
topics.context:
Phrasal verbs play a central role in how we navigate social hierarchies, express attitudes, make personal choices, and interact with peers.

### Social Hierarchy & Attitudes
- **look up to**: admire or respect someone greatly. *Young athletes look up to their coaches.*
- **look down on**: feel superior to someone. *Never look down on people in humble positions.*
- **suck up to**: flatter an authority figure excessively. *He tried to suck up to the boss.*
- **push around / pick on**: bully or unfairly criticize someone. *Do not let bullies push you around.*
- **take out on**: unfairly vent frustration onto someone. *Don't take your stress out on your family.*

### Choices, Decisions & Loyalty
- **go along with**: agree with or comply with a plan. *I will go along with the team's proposal.*
- **stick to / stick with**: remain committed to a choice or habit. *Stick to your training routine.*
- **stick together**: stay united through adversity. *Families must stick together during hard times.*
- **string along**: mislead someone with false promises. *She was just stringing him along.*
- **take up on**: accept an offer or invitation. *I will take you up on that dinner invitation.*

### Watch out!
- Do not confuse **look up to** (respect) with **look up** (search for information or visit someone).
- **Take out on** requires a direct object and "on" (e.g., *take anger out on someone*), whereas **take out** means removing something or taking someone on a date.
### Additional phrases
- **look at**: examine something, or consider it from a particular viewpoint. *The mechanic looked at the engine; let’s look at the problem another way.*
- **look over**: review or inspect something. *Could you look over my report?*
- **make up**: invent a story, or become friends again after an argument. *He made up an excuse, but they made up the next day.*
- **pick up**: learn something informally, or collect someone/something. *She picked up Italian abroad and picked up the parcel later.*
- **stick around**: stay somewhere for a while. *Stick around for coffee.*
- **stick out**: be noticeable or project beyond a surface. *Her red coat stuck out in the crowd; a nail stuck out of the board.*
- **stick up**: attach or post something visibly, or project upwards. *They stuck up a notice; a few nails stuck up from the floor.*
- **take after**: resemble an older relative. *He takes after his father.*
- **take apart**: separate something into its pieces. *She took the clock apart to clean it.*
- **take back**: return an item to a shop, or retract a statement. *I took the faulty kettle back and took back my criticism.*
- **take in**: give someone shelter, or deceive someone. *The family took in a refugee; the scam took in hundreds of people.*
- **take over**: assume control or responsibility. *Maya will take over the team next month.*

topics.title: Encounters, arrivals and unexpected events
topics.context:
Phrasal verbs are central when describing unexpected encounters, arrivals, travel movements, and sudden occurrences.

### Encounters & Arrivals
- **bump into** (= run into): meet someone unexpectedly or accidentally hit something. *I bumped into an old classmate at the supermarket.*
- **come across**: find or meet by chance; be understood or perceived in a certain way. *We came across a lovely little café in the old quarter.*
- **come by**: obtain something rare, hard to get, or in a surprising way. *How did you come by such a rare antique coin?*
- **come back**: return to a place; (of a team) recover and win; (of a fashion) become popular again. *Flared jeans have come back this year.*
- **come in**: enter a room or arrive (train, plane). *The afternoon flight from Lisbon came in on schedule.*
- **come over**: visit someone at their home, or move across a space towards someone. *Why don't you come over for dinner on Friday?*
- **get in**: arrive in town or enter a vehicle. *Our train got in late because of the heavy snow.*

### Movement & Transport
- **get on / get off**: board or leave public transport (bus, train, plane); get off (work) = finish work; get on with = continue doing. *We got on at Central Station and got off three stops later.*
- **get out**: leave a vehicle, building or other place; (of secret information) become known. *He got out of the taxi and ran into the terminal.*
- **drop off**: take someone or something to a place and leave them there; (of sales, numbers) fall. *Can you drop me off near the library?*
- **come through**: (of news, money, approval) arrive after waiting; keep a promise. *The official clearance finally came through today.*
- **come down**: (of rain) fall heavily; (of a seller) lower the price. *It's really coming down outside.*

### Unexpected Events & Situations
- **come about**: happen as a result of events. *How did this surprising change of leadership come about?*
- **come up**: arise unexpectedly or be mentioned. *I am sorry I cannot join you; an urgent issue has come up.*
- **come down to**: depend essentially on a key point. *The decision comes down to budget and available time.*
- **come off**: succeed as planned or become detached. *The surprise party came off brilliantly despite the rain.*
- **come on**: (of a light or machine) start working; (of an illness) start to develop. *I can feel a cold coming on.*
- **come out**: be published or released; (of the sun) appear. *Her new album comes out in May.*
- **come to**: total (an amount); regain consciousness. *Lunch for four came to sixty euros.*
- **come apart**: separate into pieces due to wear. *The vintage suitcase came apart at the seams.*
- **float around**: circulate as a rumor or be somewhere nearby. *A rumor has been floating around about the merger.*
- **go about**: approach or proceed with a task. *What is the best way to go about renewing my passport?*

### Watch out!
- **bump into** means to meet by accident; do not confuse with planned meetings.
- **get on** and **get off** are used for buses, trains, and planes, whereas **get in** and **get out of** are used for cars and taxis.
- **come to** can mean regain consciousness or total an amount of money.

topics.title: Coming and going, routes and access
topics.context:
Phrasal verbs built with **go** and **head** are essential for describing journeys, routes, directional movements, and decision-making about travel and plans.

### Movement, Routes & Directions
- **go around**: follow a curve, bypass an obstacle, or (of food etc.) be enough for everyone. *We went around the roadblock using a side street.*
- **go by**: pass near a place; (of time) pass; follow a rule or standard. *We watched the cycling tour go by from the balcony.*
- **go off**: (of an alarm) ring; (of an event) happen as planned; (of a path) branch off. *My alarm didn't go off this morning.*
- **head back**: start returning to where you came from. *It is getting dark, so let's head back to the lodge.*
- **head for / head toward**: move in the direction of a specific location. *The storm clouds are heading toward the coast.*
- **head into**: enter a specific area or town. *We were heading into the city center when traffic stopped.*
- **go up / go down**: move to a higher or lower level; (of prices) increase or decrease; (go down, of a computer system) stop working; (go up to someone) approach them. *We went up the winding hill to enjoy the view.*

### Departure & Return
- **go away**: leave a place, take a trip for a period, or (of a pain or problem) disappear. *They are going away for a weekend in the mountains.*
- **go back**: return to a previous place or date back in history. *I want to go back to Lisbon next spring.*
- **go out**: leave the house to socialize; (of a fire or light) stop burning or shining. *Let's go out for dinner tonight.*
- **go over**: walk across a space or visit someone nearby. *She went over to the window to open it.*

### Progress, Action & Choices
- **go after**: chase, pursue a difficult goal, or target a market. *She decided to go after her dream career.*
- **go ahead**: proceed with a plan or give permission. *You have our permission to go ahead with the project.*
- **go back on**: fail to keep a promise or agreement. *A reliable partner never goes back on their word.*
- **go for / go in for**: go for = try to achieve or choose; have something going for you = have an advantage; go in for = like and regularly do an activity. *He goes in for marathon running on weekends.*
- **go on**: continue an activity, happen, or start operating. *The meeting went on much longer than expected.*
- **go overboard**: do something excessively. *Decorating is fine, but do not go overboard on expenses.*
- **go through with**: carry out a difficult or contested plan. *Despite doubts, she went through with the purchase.*
- **go under**: go bankrupt or collapse financially. *Without financial aid, the small publisher will go under.*
- **go with**: match clothes, choose an option, or support an idea. *This navy blazer goes with almost everything.*

### Watch out!
- **head for** and **head toward** both mean traveling towards a destination, while **head back** means returning.
- **go back on** always takes an object (a promise, a word, a pledge) and means breaking it.
- **go off** can mean a path branching off, an alarm ringing, or an event going off smoothly.
